name: Euthymius the Great
knownFor: A monk from Melitene who settled in the desert near Jerusalem, baptized a Saracen chief and his people, and held to the Council of Chalcedon when most Palestinian monks turned against it.
dates: Born, by Cyril of Scythopolis, in the fourth consulship of Gratian; died, by Cyril, in the sixteenth year of the emperor Leo. The sources used here give no year in our reckoning
place: Melitene in Armenia; Jerusalem; Pharan; the Judean desert
role: Monk, priest and founder of a laura

traces: Cyril of Scythopolis says Peter, the Saracen chief Aspebetus whom Euthymius baptized, became the first bishop of the Camps in Palestine.
Cyril says the empress Eudocia, on his counsel, returned to communion with Juvenal of Jerusalem and brought many monks and lay people with her.
Cyril says the young Sabas came to him in his eighty-second year, and Euthymius sent him to Theoctistus.
remembered: Cyril of Scythopolis: a Life fit to cheer its readers and rouse them to zeal.

Louis Duchesne: after Chalcedon, when Marcian, Pulcheria and Leo of Rome wrote to the monks of Palestine, Euthymius did his best to calm them; his work to bring order to the desert monks reached only a fairly narrow circle.

uncertain: Everything told of his life comes from one source, Cyril of Scythopolis's Life, a saint's Life full of visions and wonders. Cyril names the anchorite Cyriacus as the source of some of its stories.
The Library holds the Life only in Jean-Baptiste Cotelier's Latin translation of 1681, in a rough scan; the Greek in that scan cannot be read. Every detail here was read in the Latin column.

Who baptized Aspebetus is told two ways. Cyril's Latin has Euthymius baptize him as Peter, and has Euthymius ask Juvenal of Jerusalem for a bishop. Louis Duchesne says Juvenal baptized him as Peter and made him bishop of the Saracens.
The held Latin scan gives his death in his ninety-ninth year. Cyril also says he came to Jerusalem in about his twenty-ninth year and spent sixty years in the desert. The scan is rough.
Cyril calls Theodosius, the monk who led the opposition to Chalcedon in Palestine, a deceiver. Cyril writes from the side that accepted the council.
